item.title: Lutnick ‘driving force’ behind re-engagement with Canada: sources
item.description: Multiple sources close to trade talks between Canada and the U.S. tell CTV News the “driving force” behind the scenes on re-engagement has been U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
item.dc:creator: Vassy Kapelos, Stephanie Ha
item.content:encoded: As Americans head to the polls for midterm elections Tuesday, the outcome could have significant consequences for Canada. CTVNews.ca will have live results, breaking updates, real-time election data and on-the-ground reporting from key battleground states. OTTAWA -- U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose last-minute demands led to trade talks breaking down in August, has become the behind-the-scenes “driving force” pushing Canada and the U.S. to re-engage on a deal, multiple sources tell CTV News. Sources in both countries say Lutnick initiated the re-engagement just over 10 days ago, after months of stasis, and has centred talks around the Section 232 tariffs that apply to steel, aluminum, lumber and autos because that is his purview. These are tariffs U.S. President Donald Trump imposed using a section that allows him to justify them in the name of national security. The duties in place are up to 50 per cent on steel, aluminum and copper, 25 per cent on vehicles, 10 per cent on softwood lumber and 25 per cent on certain furniture and cabinetry. Should more formalized negotiations pick back up later this week, as two sources say is a possibility, those talks could bring back into the fold U.S. Trade Rep. Jamieson Greer and involve elements outside of the Section 232 tariffs. Sources say that will likely include Keystone XL, diesel and energy exports more largely. Lutnick was a disruptive force in the last few days of negotiations between the countries back in August. Sources close to the Canadian negotiating team say he was responsible for introducing last-minute demands on culture, trade deals and autos that ultimately led to the talks breaking down in dramatic fashion at the 11th hour. Canadian government sources say their relationship with Greer during summer negotiations was much more “respectful and productive.” Lutnick’s outreach to Canada coincides — by design — with increased pressure on Trump ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday. Tariffs and the cost of living more generally have become an issue in certain key U.S. Senate races, including Michigan where the Republican candidate Mike Rogers has publicly denounced them during the campaign, despite initially being supportive. Rogers, in an interview that aired Sunday night on CBS’ “60 Minutes,” said he “doesn’t like the tariffs” on Canadian exports, and told the program he has raised the issue personally with Lutnick. Rogers also said he would be willing to support congressional efforts to override the president on tariffs if that situation was to present itself. Carney, Trump talk In a post on X Sunday, Prime Minister Mark Carney characterized the talks over the last 10 days as “constructive discussions” and said he had a “good conversation” with Trump on the future of Canada-U.S. trade. “This builds on our recent constructive discussions on the outlines of a mutually beneficial trade deal that would create jobs for our workers, boost affordability for families, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture, and sovereignty,” Carney wrote. “Our teams will now be working in the coming weeks to deliver that outcome.” Trump told reporters Sunday afternoon that they had a “concept of a very good deal with Canada.” “We’ve been losing money for many years with Canada ... many, many years, 70 to 75 years. So, we are now very close to having a deal,” he said. “I spoke with the prime minister the other day. I spoke to him again yesterday, and we have the concept of a deal that’s going to be great for our farmers, great for our country, and it’ll be fine for Canada too.” Two sources briefed on the conversations between the two leaders say the first one was 45 minutes and centred primarily on trade. The latest one was also “lengthy.” Sources on the Canadian side of negotiations are still skeptical of the president’s willingness to compromise to get a deal, though they tell CTV News the prime minister does believe Trump is serious about wanting a deal with Canada. As for what that deal might look like, sources tell CTV News discussions back in August are indicative of what Canadians should expect. Before those talks broke down, the Canadian negotiating team had landed on reduced tariffs for Canadian steel below a certain quota, a reduction in tariffs on aluminum, and provinces putting booze back on the shelves. One major sticking point was autos, which is part of why talks broke down. The U.S. offer was a reduction in tariffs to 15 per cent but only for cars and light trucks. Canada wanted that reduction extended to larger trucks manufactured in Canada. Sources say there has been some movement in discussions over the last 10 days on this, but they anticipate it will remain a difficult part of negotiations. With files from CTV News’ Graham Richardson and Marieke Walsh

item.title: Perseverance is key for a tradesperson starting their own business
item.description: The dream of starting your own business usually involves being your own boss, making your own rules and schedule, and hopefully earning more money.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: For a tradesperson, the dream of starting your own business usually involves being your own boss, making your own rules and schedule, and hopefully earning more money. The reality can include those things, but there is an entirely separate skill set and workload to consider. Sales, administration, finance, HR — you can outsource some of these functions, but the ultimate responsibility falls to you. It can also turn into a grind, said electrician Carly Steiman, between the trade labour and hustling for new work. “You’re constantly networking,” she said. “You’re constantly selling yourself, tastefully. You are constantly learning.” Steiman has been an electrician for 18 years. She incorporated herself after working in film production as a contractor and joining a film union in Toronto. The union told her there were advantages if she incorporated. “So I went to a lawyer and accountant downtown and I did all the paperwork and then I was invoicing production companies, and I was doing residential service calls,” Steiman said. Her company, Lady Electric, now serves Vancouver for residential and light commercial clients, but Steiman didn’t stop with one business. She launched the Tradeswomen Calendar & Exhibit for women in trades, a national campaign showcasing women in trades, including a touring exhibit. She also started Workbee Home Services, a home maintenance services firm to help busy families and seniors manage their properties. “I think what being an entrepreneur unlocks is when you see a problem, you don’t just complain,” Steiman said, noting that Workbee was started because she felt the so-called “sandwich generation” and seniors were enormous and underserved markets. “It breaks the ceiling that you can actually build a tool or solve the problem or improve a bottleneck. For me, I look at the economy and I’m like, ‘There is so much opportunity.’ I don’t look at the economy and complain and say, ‘There’s so many problems’ and do nothing about it.” That being said, being a business owner is humbling and arduous, Steiman added. Just getting a new business off the ground can be a lot of work, said Barbara Knoblach, a financial planner with Money Coaches Canada. A would-be entrepreneur needs to confirm there is enough demand for their work, have contacts and potential customers, have six months’ worth of expenses in savings, and ideally some jobs already lined up, as well as working capital to get a business started, she said in an email interview. Aside from assembling your professional team — bookkeeper, accountant and financial planner, for instance — it’s also critical to charge enough for your work, Knoblach added. “Depending on your trade, you may have considerable expenses for tools, equipment, vehicles, subcontractors, insurance and materials,” she said. “You also need to account for the time you spend on work that cannot be billed directly to your customers. If you don’t take these expenses into consideration, you may end up working very hard without making much money.” You should also review options for health benefits and disability insurance. Without employer benefits, Knoblach said, you have to protect your health and income in case of illness or injury. New business owners will frequently find themselves navigating novel scenarios, Knoblach said. If you have employees, what will you do if they call in sick before a big job? What happens when business slows down, or if customers are late to pay? “At the same time, your operating expenses continue,” Knoblach pointed out. Ultimately, she felt tradespeople should be cautious in starting their own company, with full awareness of the financial implications and workload. If you succeed, it is a rewarding path, Knoblach said — but it is not an easy one. “Being good at your trade does not necessarily mean you will also be successful at running a business,” she said. “These are two different things.” There are other options for running a company rather than just starting solo, Steiman noted. Small trades companies — “mom and pop shops” with few employees — might be willing to sell the business when the owners retire. Whatever the path, and despite all the work, owning your own business has many perks, Steiman said. You can choose the jobs you take on, you can have your own culture and values, you can be a leader in the community, you can be a mentor in the industry, you can figure out your own margins, you can work with others if you want, or work alone if you prefer. Steiman sees many opportunities out there for entrepreneurship and trades. “I think a lot of people that are going to be successful are going to embody perseverance — and that is showing up every day, waking up early, having a day planner, being organized, being on it, and being self-determined,” she said. “If you are somebody with those qualities, then no matter what you do in life, you will be successful. And if you decide to become an entrepreneur, you will be very successful.” --- Nina Dragicevic, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

item.title: Federal budget is about 'changing Canada's growth model,' finance minister says
item.description: Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne says the federal budget he will table later this week is about “changing Canada’s growth model.” ...
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne says the federal budget he will table later this week is about “changing Canada’s growth model.” Champagne spoke at the Canadian Club Toronto over breakfast today to give business leaders a preview of what to expect in Thursday’s federal budget. He said the government is focused on unlocking private investment and boosting productivity, which has lagged for years in many sectors of the economy. Champagne suggested the budget will talk about how new tax incentives can help small businesses. He said the big-ticket measures to spur investment, like the productivity mega-deduction, can both help a local café buy a new coffee machine and help get shovels in the ground for an oil pipeline. The finance minister did not answer directly when asked whether the upcoming budget will offer further details about a planned sovereign wealth fund or a proposal to open Canada’s airports up to private investment. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.
